name: Bastion
tagline: Your network gets attacked every day — now it fights back
description: Bastion runs continuous, autonomous penetration tests against your infrastructure so you find the holes before attackers do. No more annual pen tests that are outdated the day after the report lands.
mission:
Annual penetration tests are a relic. You pay a consultancy six figures, wait three weeks for a PDF, patch the critical findings, and then spend the next eleven months hoping nothing new has broken. Meanwhile, your attack surface changes every time someone pushes code, spins up a cloud instance, or adds an integration.

Bastion was built by red teamers who got tired of writing the same reports for the same clients year after year. We took the methodology of a skilled human pentester — reconnaissance, enumeration, exploitation, lateral movement, reporting — and turned it into a platform that runs continuously against your live infrastructure. Not a vulnerability scanner. An actual attack simulation engine that thinks like an adversary.

Our philosophy is simple: defense without offense is guesswork. You can't know if your controls work until something tries to break them. Bastion tries to break them every single day, then tells you exactly what it found, how it got in, and what to fix first.

We're a team of former offensive security researchers from Mandiant, NCC Group, and the US Cyber Command. We've spent careers breaking into organizations and we believe that capability should be democratized — not locked behind $200K consulting engagements that happen once a year.
marketResearch:
The penetration testing market is valued at $3.1B in 2025, growing at 13.2% CAGR. The shift toward continuous security validation — sometimes called breach and attack simulation (BAS) — represents a $1.4B sub-segment growing at 28% CAGR as organizations move away from point-in-time assessments. Our TAM is $1.4B, SAM is $520M targeting mid-market and enterprise companies in North America and Europe, and initial SOM is $85M.

Competitors include legacy pen test firms (Bishop Fox, Rapid7), vulnerability scanners (Qualys, Tenable) that lack exploitation capability, and BAS platforms (SafeBreach, AttackIQ, Pentera). Bastion differentiates by combining real exploitation with continuous cadence — we don't simulate attacks, we execute them safely using containment boundaries and rollback mechanisms. Our finding severity accuracy is 94% vs. the 60-70% typical of scanner-based approaches.

Primary buyers are CISOs and security engineering leads at companies with 200-5,000 employees, particularly in fintech, healthcare, and SaaS. The pain point is universal: compliance mandates require pen testing, but annual assessments provide a false sense of security. Early traction includes 38 customers, $1.9M ARR, and partnerships with two cyber insurance providers who offer premium discounts to Bastion users.

name: Clause
tagline: Contracts shouldn't be the reason your deal stalls
description: Clause is a contract lifecycle management platform built specifically for startups and scaling companies. From template creation to e-signature to renewal tracking, it replaces the messy mix of Google Docs, email threads, and forgotten deadlines that most early-stage legal teams rely on.
mission:
At most startups, the "contract process" looks like this: someone duplicates a Google Doc, changes the company name in three places (but misses the fourth), emails it to the counterparty, loses track of which version has the latest redlines, and eventually signs something nobody is entirely sure matches what was negotiated. The signed PDF goes into a folder nobody will open again until something goes wrong.

Clause exists because contracts are too important to manage this way. They define your revenue, your liability, your IP ownership, and your vendor relationships. Yet most companies don't invest in contract infrastructure until they've already been burned — by a missed renewal that auto-renewed for two years, by an indemnification clause nobody caught, or by a customer claiming terms that aren't in the signed version.

We're not building for BigLaw or Fortune 500 legal departments. We're building for the startup GC who is also the head of HR and the compliance officer. For the founder who signs 30 contracts a quarter without a lawyer on staff. For the ops lead who just needs a vendor NDA that doesn't take three weeks to close.

Our platform handles the full lifecycle — template library, clause bank, approval workflows, e-signature, obligation tracking, and renewal alerts — in a product that feels like Notion, not SAP. We believe contract management should be as intuitive as the tools startups already love.
marketResearch:
The CLM market is projected to reach $7.7B by 2030, growing at 14.9% CAGR. However, the vast majority of CLM spend is concentrated in enterprise (1,000+ employees), leaving a massive underserved segment of startups and mid-market companies. Our TAM for SMB and mid-market CLM is $2.1B, SAM targeting companies with 20-500 employees in North America is $680M, and initial SOM is $95M.

Enterprise CLM tools (Ironclad, Icertis, Agiloft) are powerful but require months of implementation and cost $50K-$500K annually. Startup-friendly tools (SpotDraft, Juro, Precisely) are growing but still emphasize feature complexity over simplicity. Clause differentiates through radical simplicity — 15-minute setup, pre-built template libraries by industry, and a pricing model that starts at $0 for up to 10 contracts per month.

Our target buyer is the first legal hire, head of operations, or founder at companies with 20-200 employees. The trigger event is typically crossing 50+ active contracts where Google Docs and email become unmanageable. Early traction: 220 companies, $890K ARR, 91% retention. Our PLG funnel converts 14% of free users to paid within 60 days, driven by the renewal alert feature that immediately demonstrates value when it catches a forgotten auto-renewal.

name: Ember HR
tagline: You can't fix culture if you can't see it
description: Ember HR measures what surveys miss — the real-time engagement, collaboration patterns, and sentiment signals that reveal whether your remote team is thriving or quietly burning out. Think of it as a health dashboard for your company culture.
mission:
Remote work solved the commute problem and created a visibility problem. When your team was in an office, you could feel the energy — the hallway conversations, the lunch table debates, the subtle shift when morale started dipping. Now that signal is gone, replaced by green dots on Slack and an annual engagement survey that tells you what people felt six months ago.

Ember HR was born from a conviction that culture isn't something you measure once a year. It's a living system that shifts weekly, sometimes daily, and the companies that thrive remotely are the ones that can see those shifts as they happen. Not through surveillance — through signal.

We aggregate anonymized data from the tools your team already uses — communication patterns, meeting loads, collaboration networks, recognition frequency, response times — and surface the cultural signals hidden in the noise. Which teams are siloed? Where is meeting fatigue concentrated? Are new hires integrating into the collaboration network or staying isolated?

Our founding team includes organizational psychologists and data scientists who spent years studying what makes distributed teams work. We believe the future of HR isn't more surveys — it's passive, ethical sensing that gives people leaders the context to act before problems become crises.

The employee engagement and analytics market is valued at $1.5B, growing at 15% CAGR as remote and hybrid work become permanent. Our TAM is $1.5B, SAM targeting remote-first and hybrid companies with 50-2,000 employees is $480M, and SOM is $72M.

Competitors include survey-based platforms (Culture Amp, Lattice, 15Five) that rely on active employee participation, and workforce analytics tools (Microsoft Viva Insights, Worklytics) that focus on productivity metrics rather than cultural health. Ember differentiates by combining passive behavioral signals with AI-driven cultural analysis — no survey fatigue, no self-report bias, and insights that update weekly rather than quarterly.

The trigger event is usually a retention crisis or a failed engagement survey that revealed problems too late to prevent departures. name: Sentinel
tagline: Compliance that watches while you build
description: Sentinel monitors your fintech infrastructure in real time against regulatory requirements — SOX, PCI-DSS, SOC 2, state money transmitter laws — and alerts you the moment something drifts out of compliance. No more quarterly audits revealing surprises from three months ago.
mission:
Fintech compliance is a paradox. You need to move fast to compete, but every new feature, every infrastructure change, every third-party integration can push you out of compliance with regulations that carry seven-figure penalties. Most fintech companies discover compliance gaps the worst possible way: during an audit, during a breach investigation, or when a regulator comes knocking.

Sentinel was founded by compliance engineers and former bank examiners who watched fintech after fintech fail the same way — not because they didn't care about compliance, but because they couldn't see it in real time. Their compliance posture was a snapshot taken during the last audit, not a live signal.

We built Sentinel to make compliance observable. Our platform continuously monitors your infrastructure, code deployments, access controls, data flows, and vendor connections against the specific regulatory frameworks that apply to your business. When something drifts — a new S3 bucket without encryption, an access policy that violates SOX segregation of duties, a data flow that crosses a jurisdictional boundary — Sentinel flags it in minutes, not months.

Our vision is a world where compliance is a CI/CD check, not a quarterly fire drill. Where every deploy is validated against regulatory requirements before it hits production. Where your compliance team spends their time on strategic risk management, not manual evidence collection.

Our TAM is $6.2B, SAM is $1.8B targeting fintech companies in North America with $10M+ in annual payment volume, and SOM is $180M.

Sentinel differentiates by combining infrastructure-level monitoring with financial regulatory expertise — we understand both your Kubernetes cluster and your state money transmitter obligations.

name: Redline
tagline: Negotiate contracts like you've read a thousand of them — because we have
description: Redline is a contract redlining tool that reads agreements, compares them against market standards and your company's positions, and suggests specific edits with plain-language explanations. It's the senior associate who never sleeps and has reviewed every contract type.
mission:
Contract negotiation is one of the last business processes where the quality of the output depends almost entirely on the experience of the individual doing the work. A first-year associate reviewing an MSA will miss things a tenth-year partner catches instantly — not because they're careless, but because pattern recognition takes thousands of reps to develop.

Redline compresses that learning curve to zero. Our platform reads incoming contracts, identifies clauses that deviate from market norms or your company's preferred positions, and suggests specific redline edits with natural-language explanations of why each change matters. Not flags. Not risk scores. Actual suggested language that your team can accept, modify, or reject with full context.

We built Redline because we watched brilliant lawyers spend hours on mechanical analysis that machines can do in seconds, while the strategic work — the creative structuring, the relationship navigation, the judgment calls — went under-resourced. We want every lawyer to negotiate like a senior partner from day one.

Our approach is fundamentally different from contract review tools that just highlight risks. Highlighting a problem without suggesting a solution creates more work, not less. Redline provides the solution: specific counter-language, calibrated to your company's risk tolerance, benchmarked against what similarly-situated companies accept in comparable deals.

name: Tessera
tagline: Hire for what people can do, not where they went to school
description: Tessera is a skills-based hiring platform that replaces resume screening with structured skill assessments and blind evaluation. It removes the biases baked into traditional hiring — school name, employer brand, gaps in employment — and surfaces candidates based on demonstrated ability.
mission:
The resume is a terrible predictor of job performance. Study after study shows that unstructured resume screening introduces bias at every level — against women, against minorities, against career changers, against anyone whose path doesn't match the recruiter's mental model of what a "good" candidate looks like. And yet resumes remain the foundation of nearly every hiring process on Earth.

Tessera was founded on a radical but evidence-backed premise: if you evaluate candidates on what they can do instead of where they've been, you get better hires and more diverse teams simultaneously. These aren't competing goals — they're the same goal, because bias is noise, and removing noise improves signal.

Our platform replaces the resume screen with structured skill evaluations designed by I/O psychologists and calibrated to actual job performance. Candidates complete relevant assessments — coding challenges, writing samples, case analyses, design exercises — and their work is evaluated blindly by reviewers who never see a name, photo, school, or employer. Only skills and demonstrated ability.

We're not anti-resume as a philosophical stance. We're anti-resume because the data is overwhelming: structured skill evaluation predicts job performance 2-4x better than resume screening. Companies that switch to skills-based hiring see broader talent pools, faster time-to-hire, higher offer acceptance rates, and dramatically better diversity outcomes. It's not a trade-off. It's strictly better.
marketResearch:
The global recruiting software market is $3.2B, projected to reach $5.3B by 2030 at 7.5% CAGR. Within this, skills-based hiring platforms are the fastest-growing segment at 28% CAGR, driven by increasing recognition that traditional screening methods underperform and introduce bias. TAM is $3.2B, SAM targeting mid-market and enterprise companies in North America committed to skills-based hiring is $920M, SOM is $105M.

Competitors include assessment platforms (HackerRank, Codility) focused only on technical roles, ATS tools (Greenhouse, Lever) that bolt on basic screening, and emerging skills platforms (Eightfold, Beamery) focused on internal mobility rather than external hiring. Tessera differentiates by covering all role types — not just engineering — with blind evaluation built into the core workflow rather than added as an optional step.

Target buyers are VPs of Talent, Heads of DEI, and CHROs at companies with 200+ employees actively committed to reducing bias in hiring. Our sales trigger is typically a failed diversity initiative or a realization that existing processes aren't delivering diverse candidate slates. Early traction: 64 companies, $980K ARR, with customers reporting 3.2x more diverse finalist slates and 28% improvement in 12-month retention for skills-based hires vs. resume-screened hires.

name: Lockstep
tagline: Know what's in your supply chain before attackers do
description: Lockstep scans your open-source dependencies for security vulnerabilities, malicious packages, license risks, and maintainer health signals. It goes beyond CVE databases to assess the actual risk of every package in your dependency tree.
mission:
The average modern application has over 1,200 dependencies. Most engineering teams can name maybe a dozen of them. The rest are transitive — pulled in by libraries that pulled in other libraries — forming an invisible supply chain that nobody audited and everybody trusts implicitly.

Then Log4Shell happened. Then the ua-parser-js compromise. Then the colors.js sabotage. Each incident reminded the industry of something supply chain security researchers had been saying for years: your application is only as secure as your least-maintained transitive dependency.

Lockstep was founded to make supply chain risk visible and manageable. We don't just check CVE databases — that's table stakes. We analyze maintainer activity, funding status, bus factor, known vulnerabilities in transitive deps, typosquatting risk, behavioral anomalies in recent releases, and license compliance across your entire dependency tree. The question isn't just "is this package vulnerable?" — it's "should you trust this package at all?"

Our founding team built dependency management systems at npm and GitHub, and we saw firsthand how little visibility most organizations had into what they were actually shipping. We're building the supply chain intelligence layer that every engineering organization needs but almost none have today.
marketResearch:
The software supply chain security market is valued at $2.8B in 2025, growing at 31% CAGR — one of the fastest-growing segments in cybersecurity. Executive orders mandating SBOMs (Software Bill of Materials) and increasing insurance requirements are accelerating adoption. TAM is $2.8B, SAM targeting engineering organizations with 20+ developers shipping production software is $1.1B, SOM is $140M.

Competitors include vulnerability scanners (Snyk, Mend.io, Dependabot) that focus primarily on known CVEs, SBOM tools (Anchore, Syft) that catalog without assessing risk, and emerging supply chain platforms (Socket.dev, Phylum) with overlapping but narrower scope. Lockstep differentiates through depth of analysis — we assess 14 risk signals per package vs. the 2-3 that CVE-focused tools check — and through our maintainer health scoring, which predicts abandonment and compromise risk before incidents occur.

Target buyers are security engineering leads and VP Engineering at software companies with 50+ engineers. The sales trigger is typically a supply chain incident (their own or a high-profile public one) or a compliance mandate requiring SBOMs. Early traction: 92 companies, $1.7M ARR, scanning 340M+ packages monthly. Our open-source CLI drives bottom-up adoption, converting 18% of active users to paid team plans within 120 days.

name: Arbiter
tagline: Resolve disputes in days, not months
description: Arbiter is an online dispute resolution platform for e-commerce marketplaces, SaaS companies, and digital platforms. When buyers and sellers disagree, Arbiter provides structured negotiation, mediation, and binding resolution — all without lawyers, courts, or months of waiting.
mission:
E-commerce is a $6 trillion industry running on a dispute resolution system designed for the physical world. When a buyer and seller disagree about a transaction — the item wasn't as described, the service wasn't delivered, the refund wasn't processed — the options are bleak: a credit card chargeback (adversarial, expensive, and binary), small claims court (slow, inaccessible, and impractical for cross-border transactions), or eating the loss and leaving a bad review.

Arbiter was built to give digital commerce a native dispute resolution layer. Our platform guides both parties through a structured process — first attempting automated resolution based on platform policies, then offering mediated negotiation with AI assistance, and finally providing binding arbitration by qualified human neutrals when needed. The entire process happens online, typically resolves in 3-5 days, and costs a fraction of traditional alternatives.

We believe that trust is the infrastructure of commerce. Marketplaces that resolve disputes fairly and quickly see higher buyer confidence, higher seller retention, and fewer chargebacks. Our mission is to make fair resolution accessible to every transaction, regardless of size or geography.

Our founding team includes former eBay dispute resolution architects, AAA arbitrators, and marketplace operators. We've collectively resolved over 2 million disputes and we're bringing that expertise to every platform that needs it.
marketResearch:
The online dispute resolution (ODR) market is valued at $890M in 2025, projected to reach $3.2B by 2030 at 29% CAGR. Growth is driven by the explosion of e-commerce, increasing cross-border transactions, and platform liability regulations like the EU's Digital Services Act. TAM is $3.2B, SAM targeting e-commerce marketplaces and digital platforms processing $10M+ in annual GMV is $840M, SOM is $95M.

Competitors include traditional arbitration bodies (AAA, JAMS) adapting to online formats but lacking platform integration, chargeback management tools (Chargebacks911, Midigator) that address symptoms rather than root causes, and marketplace-native systems (eBay, Amazon) that are proprietary and unavailable to other platforms. Arbiter differentiates by offering embeddable dispute resolution as an API — marketplaces integrate our system into their existing workflow without building their own.

Target buyers are marketplace operations leads, trust & safety teams, and platform product managers at companies processing 1,000+ monthly transactions. The pain points are chargebacks (costing platforms 1-2% of GMV), customer churn from poor dispute experience, and regulatory pressure for fair resolution mechanisms. Early traction: 18 platforms integrated, $720K ARR, resolving 12,000+ disputes per month with an average resolution time of 3.8 days and 87% mutual satisfaction rate.

name: Cadre
tagline: Equity shouldn't require a law degree to understand
description: Cadre is an employee equity management platform for startups. It handles cap table management, offer letter generation, vesting schedules, 409A valuations, and employee equity education — so founders stop explaining stock options on napkins and employees actually understand what they own.
mission:
Startup equity is broken — not the concept, but the execution. Founders grant options without understanding dilution. Employees accept equity packages without grasping vesting cliffs, exercise windows, or tax implications. Early hires leave money on the table because nobody explained the difference between ISOs and NSOs. And the cap table lives in a spreadsheet that hasn't been reconciled since the seed round.

Cadre exists because equity is the most powerful tool startups have for attracting and retaining talent, and it's being wasted by bad tooling and worse communication. We've built a platform that handles the mechanics — cap table management, option grants, vesting tracking, 409A valuations, exercise workflows — and, just as importantly, the education. Every employee gets a personalized equity dashboard that shows what they own, what it could be worth, and what decisions they need to make (and when).

We're a team of former startup CFOs, equity compensation lawyers, and product designers who watched the same equity literacy gap cause problems at every company we worked at. The engineer who didn't exercise before the 90-day window. The early employee who didn't understand their tax obligation. The founder who accidentally issued more shares than authorized.

Our mission is to make equity work the way it was supposed to: as a genuine wealth-creation mechanism that aligns incentives, attracts exceptional people, and rewards the risk of joining early. That only happens when everyone — founders, employees, and investors — can see the same clear picture.
marketResearch:
The equity management software market is valued at $620M in 2025, projected to reach $1.8B by 2030 at 23% CAGR. Growth is driven by the increasing use of equity compensation beyond tech (healthcare, biotech, professional services), regulatory changes around equity tax treatment, and the sheer volume of VC-backed startups granting options. TAM is $1.8B, SAM targeting VC-backed startups with 10-500 employees in North America is $520M, SOM is $68M.

Competitors include Carta (dominant incumbent, $7.4B valuation but increasingly expensive and enterprise-focused), Pulley (strong SMB challenger, narrower feature set), and Shareworks/E*Trade (enterprise, post-IPO focus). Cadre differentiates through two dimensions: radical simplicity for early-stage companies (setup in under an hour, not weeks) and best-in-class employee equity education (personalized dashboards, tax scenario modeling, exercise decision guidance).

Target buyers are founders, CFOs, and heads of people at VC-backed startups from seed through Series C. The trigger event is typically hiring employee #10-20 when equity administration becomes too complex for spreadsheets. Early traction: 180 companies, $1.1M ARR, managing $2.4B in total equity value. Our PLG motion starts with a free cap table tool for up to 20 stakeholders, converting 26% to paid when companies need option grants, 409A valuations, or employee portals.

name: Perimeter
tagline: Zero trust that doesn't make your team want to quit
description: Perimeter is a zero-trust network access platform built for remote-first companies. It replaces VPNs with identity-based access controls that are invisible when they should be and ironclad when they need to be. Security without the friction.
mission:
VPNs were designed for a world where the office was the perimeter. You connected to the corporate network and you were "inside" — trusted to access everything. That model was already crumbling when remote work accelerated its collapse. Now your "network" is 400 employees on home wifi, coffee shop connections, and airport lounges, and the VPN is a bottleneck that everyone hates and many bypass.

Perimeter replaces the VPN with zero-trust network access — the principle that no user, device, or connection is inherently trusted. Every access request is verified against identity, device health, location, behavior patterns, and the specific resource being requested. The result is security that's simultaneously stronger and less annoying than a VPN.

We built Perimeter because we watched security teams deploy zero-trust architectures that were technically sound and operationally miserable. Constant MFA prompts. Broken workflows. Developers who couldn't access staging because their device score dropped. Zero trust doesn't have to mean zero productivity.

Our approach is invisible by default and strict when it matters. Accessing your normal tools from your managed device on your home network? Seamless. Accessing the production database from an unrecognized device in a new country? That's when Perimeter asks questions. Context-aware security that adapts its posture to actual risk, not blanket paranoia.
marketResearch:
The zero-trust security market is valued at $31.6B in 2025, projected to reach $67B by 2030 at 16.5% CAGR. The ZTNA sub-segment specifically — replacing VPNs with identity-based access — is $4.8B and growing at 25% CAGR. TAM is $4.8B, SAM targeting remote-first and hybrid companies with 50-5,000 employees is $1.6B, SOM is $190M.

Competitors include established ZTNA vendors (Zscaler, Cloudflare Access, Palo Alto Prisma) that are powerful but complex and enterprise-priced, and newer entrants (Tailscale, Twingate) that simplify access but offer limited policy engines. Perimeter differentiates by combining frictionless user experience with deep policy controls — context-aware access that adapts to risk signals in real time without interrupting low-risk workflows.

Target buyers are CISOs, IT leads, and heads of remote at companies with 100-2,000 remote employees. The pain point is universal: VPNs are a security liability and a productivity drain. The trigger event is usually a security incident traced to VPN credentials, or a new CISO mandate to implement zero trust. Early traction: 56 companies, $2.8M ARR, 98% user adoption rate (vs. 60-70% typical for VPN). Our free tier for up to 10 users drives bottom-up adoption in engineering teams, expanding to company-wide deployment.
